summary: Sets out requirements for Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO), a service that gives applications guidance when choosing among several equivalent hosts, such as peers in file sharing. The aim is to help applications pick well-placed sources while reducing wasted traffic on networks. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: ALTO is intended to give applications guidance when they choose among several hosts that can provide the same resource. This RFC lists requirements for how that guidance should be requested, delivered, and protected.

questions: how can applications choose the best peer
how does alto help choose a host
what are the two alto query modes
subtitle: Requirements for a service that helps applications choose among equivalent network hosts.

tldr.problem: Applications may choose among equivalent servers or peers without knowing network information that could improve performance and reduce network use.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists requirements for ALTO client protocols, host descriptions, rating criteria, server discovery, extensibility, and privacy and security.
tldr.outcome: This Informational document is a requirements list, not an ALTO protocol specification. It is intended to guide the specification and assessment of protocols and implementations.

today: RFC 6708 is an Informational requirements document published in September 2012. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the RFC leaves the detailed ALTO protocol specifications out of scope.

sections.title: The Purpose of ALTO
sections.content:
Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) gives applications information to help select a host from several candidates that can provide the same resource. The document identifies peer-to-peer applications as one use, and also describes selecting among servers or replicas and choosing a media relay.

The guidance can reflect factors such as topological distance, network costs, or provider policies. ALTO entities provide guidance but do not relay the user data. This RFC lists requirements for ALTO protocols and discovery mechanisms; it does not define a specific architecture or protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: ALTO helps an application choose which suitable host to contact. This document describes what an ALTO protocol must support, rather than defining the protocol itself.

sections.title: Host Descriptions and Rating Criteria
sections.content:
A host-group descriptor identifies one or more hosts and their place in the network. The RFC gives examples such as an IP address, an address prefix or range, and an Autonomous System number. A rating criterion describes what counts as a better candidate, such as lower topological distance or an operator's preference.

A host-characteristics attribute describes another property of a host, such as whether its Internet access has flat-rate charging. The RFC requires support for IPv4 and IPv6 prefixes and expects other descriptor types to have a way to map to IP prefixes. It does not require ALTO to reveal how an operator calculates its ratings.
sections.plainLanguage: The system needs a way to name candidate hosts and a rule for ranking them. The network may provide useful properties without revealing its full internal map.

sections.title: Client Protocol and Query Modes
sections.content:
An ALTO client protocol must carry queries and replies, support operations and management, allow backward-compatible extensions, and use a congestion-aware transport. It must support clients embedded in a resource consumer and clients in a third party that asks on the consumer's behalf. The service may be provided by an organization other than the network operator.

The RFC describes target-aware queries, which send known candidate hosts to the server for ranking, and target-independent queries, which retrieve guidance in advance for local use. A protocol must specify at least one mode and should specify both. It should also support freshness information and say how responses may be reused.
sections.plainLanguage: An application can ask about known candidates or download guidance for later use. A protocol must define at least one of these query styles and should explain when stored guidance remains valid.

sections.title: Finding ALTO Servers
sections.content:
Clients need a discovery mechanism to find one or more ALTO servers. The requirements cover clients finding servers for themselves and third-party clients finding servers for remote consumers. Both kinds of discovery must work when the client or consumer is behind a Network Address Translator (NAT).

The RFC recommends reusing existing discovery methods such as DNS, DHCP, or PPP configuration. Discovery should be able to return multiple servers and indicate preferences among them. The document leaves the specific discovery protocol out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Before requesting guidance, a client must find a suitable ALTO server. The requirements favor discovery methods that can return several choices and work through address translation.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
A client protocol specification must define how clients and servers are authenticated, how messages are encrypted, and how the service is protected from denial-of-service attacks. It must support different levels of detail so queries and replies can limit sensitive information. A client need not prevent redistribution of information it receives.

The RFC identifies risks for both network operators and users. An operator may reveal topology or policy; a query may reveal which resources a user seeks. Authentication and encryption do not prevent authorized clients from sharing or combining responses, so operators should only provide information they are willing to disclose in those ways.
sections.plainLanguage: ALTO queries can reveal user interests, and replies can reveal network details. Security controls can limit access and protect messages, but they cannot stop clients from sharing information they receive.
